quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-01.title: Normal closures
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-01.body:
For $g\in G$ write $g^G$ for its conjugacy class. The subgroup $\langle g^G\rangle$ is normal (its generating set is closed under conjugation) and it is the smallest normal subgroup containing $g$.

**(i)** Let $G=\langle K\rangle$ with $K=g^G$. In $G/G'$ conjugate elements have the same image, since $h^{-1}gh=g[g,h]$. So $G/G'$ is generated by the single element $gG'$, hence cyclic.

**(ii)** If some $g$ lies in no proper normal subgroup, then the normal subgroup $\langle g^G\rangle$ containing $g$ must be $G$, so $G$ has $*$. Conversely, suppose $G=\langle g^G\rangle$ and $g\in N\trianglelefteq G$. Then $g^G\subseteq N$, so $G=\langle g^G\rangle\subseteq N$, i.e. $N=G$. So $g$ is not in the union of the proper normal subgroups. Thus $G$ has $*$ iff some element lies outside every proper normal subgroup, i.e. iff $G$ is not the union of its proper normal subgroups.

**(iii)** *Hint.* Let $L\trianglelefteq G$ with $N\not\subseteq L$. Then $L\cap N\trianglelefteq N$ is a proper normal subgroup of the simple group $N$, so $L\cap N=1$. Hence $[L,N]\subseteq L\cap N=1$ (both are normal), so $L\subseteq C_G(N)$. In $G=N\times M$, $C_G(N)=Z(N)\times M=M$ because the nonabelian simple group $N$ has trivial center. So $L\subseteq M$.

By (ii) applied to $M$, pick $m\in M$ lying in no proper normal subgroup of $M$, and pick $1\ne n\in N$. Put $g=nm$ (i.e. $(n,m)$). Let $L\trianglelefteq G$ contain $g$.
- If $N\not\subseteq L$, then $L\subseteq M$ by the hint, but $g\notin M$ since $n\ne1$; impossible.
- If $N\subseteq L$, then $m=n^{-1}g\in L\cap M$. Now $L\cap M$ is normal in $G$, hence in $M$, and contains $m$, so $L\cap M=M$. Thus $L\supseteq NM=G$.

So $g$ lies in no proper normal subgroup of $G$, and by (ii) $G$ has property $*$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-02.title: The colon ideal
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-02.body:
**(i)** Let $M=mR$ be maximal and let $I$ be an ideal with $M^2\subseteq I\subseteq M$. Every element of $I$ has the form $rm$. Put $J=\{r\in R\mid rm\in I\}$, an ideal of $R$. Since $M\cdot m\subseteq M^2\subseteq I$, we have $M\subseteq J$, so $J=M$ or $J=R$ by maximality.
- If $J=R$, then $m\in I$, so $M=mR\subseteq I$ and $I=M$.
- If $J=M$, then $I=\{rm\mid r\in J\}=Mm=M^2$.

So no ideal lies strictly between $M^2$ and $M$.

**(ii)** *Maximal but not principal.* $R=F[x,y]$ ($F$ a field), $M=(x,y)$ (maximal, as $R/M\cong F$), $M^2=(x^2,xy,y^2)$, and $I=(x,y^2)$. Then $I\supsetneq M^2$ since $x\notin M^2$ (every element of $M^2$ has no terms of degree $<2$), and $I\subsetneq M$ since $y\notin I$ (every element of $I$ is $xa+y^2b$, whose linear part is a multiple of $x$).

*Principal but not maximal.* $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $M=(4)$, $M^2=(16)$, $I=(8)$: $(4)\supsetneq(8)\supsetneq(16)$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-03.title: Coefficients are algebraic
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-03.body:
Let $n=|E:L|$ and fix an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $E$.

**(i)** Let $\alpha\in K$ with minimal polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$. Suppose $f=gh$ in $L[x]$ with $g$ monic. In $\Omega[x]$, $f=\prod(x-\alpha_i)$ with all $\alpha_i$ algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and by unique factorization $g$ is a product of some of the $x-\alpha_i$. Hence the coefficients of $g$ are (elementary symmetric) polynomials in some $\alpha_i$, so they are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$. They also lie in $L\subseteq E$, so they lie in $K\cap L=\mathbb{Q}$. Thus $g\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ divides $f$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$, and irreducibility of $f$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ forces $g=1$ or $g=f$. So $f$ is irreducible over $L$, hence is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $L$, and
$$|\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|=\deg f=|L[\alpha]:L|\le|E:L|=n,$$
since $L\subseteq L[\alpha]\subseteq E$.

**(ii)** Among the subfields $M\subseteq K$ with $|M:\mathbb{Q}|\le n$ (e.g. $\mathbb{Q}$), choose one of maximal degree. Let $\alpha\in K$. Then $M[\alpha]\subseteq K$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, and since we are in characteristic $0$ the primitive element theorem gives $M[\alpha]=\mathbb{Q}[\gamma]$ for some $\gamma\in K$. By (i), $|M[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|=|\mathbb{Q}[\gamma]:\mathbb{Q}|\le n$. Since $M\subseteq M[\alpha]$ and $M$ has maximal degree among such fields, $|M[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|=|M:\mathbb{Q}|$, so $M[\alpha]=M$ and $\alpha\in M$. Hence $K=M$ and $|K:\mathbb{Q}|\le n=|E:L|$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-04.title: Commutation relation
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-04.body:
**(i)** We claim $TS^n=S^nT+nS^n$ for all $n\ge0$. For $n=0$ it is trivial. If it holds for $n$, then using $TS=ST+S$,
$$TS^{n+1}=(TS)S^n=(ST+S)S^n=S(TS^n)+S^{n+1}=S(S^nT+nS^n)+S^{n+1}=S^{n+1}T+(n+1)S^{n+1}.$$
Applying this to $v$ with $Tv=0$: $T(S^nv)=n\,S^nv$. Since $S$ is injective and $v\ne0$, $S^nv\ne0$. So $S^nv$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $n\cdot1_K$.

**(ii)** If $\mathrm{char}\,K=0$, the scalars $0,1,2,\dots$ are pairwise distinct. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so $v,Sv,S^2v,\dots$ are linearly independent and $\dim V=\infty$.

**(iii)** Let $K=\mathbb{F}_3$, $V=K^3$ with basis $v_0,v_1,v_2$, and define $S(v_i)=v_{i+1}$ (indices mod 3) and $T(v_i)=i\,v_i$. $S$ permutes a basis, so it is one-to-one, and $T(v_0)=0$ with $v_0\ne0$. Check $TS-ST=S$ on the basis: $(TS-ST)(v_i)=T(v_{i+1})-iS(v_i)=\big((i+1)-i\big)v_{i+1}=v_{i+1}=S(v_i)$ for $i=0,1$, and for $i=2$: $T(v_0)-2v_0=0-2v_0=v_0=S(v_2)$ because $-2=1$ in $\mathbb{F}_3$. In matrices (columns = images): $S=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $T=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,2)$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-05.title: Roots of unity in finite fields
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-05.body:
Every root $\zeta$ of $f$ (in any extension) satisfies $\zeta^5=1$, since $(x-1)f(x)=x^5-1$.

**(i)** Suppose $\zeta\in F$ is a root. If $\zeta\ne1$, its multiplicative order divides $5$ and is not $1$, so it is $5$; then $\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3,\zeta^4$ are four distinct elements of $F$, each a root of $x^5-1$ different from $1$, hence roots of $f$; so $f=\prod_{i=1}^4(x-\zeta^i)$ splits over $F$. If $\zeta=1$, then $0=f(1)=5$ in $F$, so $\mathrm{char}F=5$ and $f=(x^5-1)/(x-1)=(x-1)^5/(x-1)=(x-1)^4$ splits.

So $f$ has a root in $F$ iff either $\mathrm{char}F=5$ (i.e. $q\equiv0\bmod5$) or $F^\times$ contains an element of order $5$. As $F^\times$ is cyclic of order $q-1$, the latter holds iff $5\mid q-1$. Hence $f$ has a root (equivalently, splits) iff $q\equiv0$ or $1\pmod5$.

**(ii)** If $g$ is an irreducible quadratic factor, then $f$ has no root in $F$ (otherwise it would split into linear factors by (i), and $g$ could not be an irreducible factor). In particular $\mathrm{char}F\neq5$ and $F^\times$ has no element of order $5$. Over a splitting field, $g=(x-\beta)(x-\beta')$ with $\beta^5=\beta'^5=1$, so its constant term $c=\beta\beta'\in F$ satisfies $c^5=1$. Hence $c=1$.

**(iii)** $29\equiv4\pmod5$, so $f$ has no roots in $\mathbb{F}_{29}$; but $29^2\equiv1\pmod5$, so the roots lie in $\mathbb{F}_{29^2}$ and $f$ is a product of two irreducible quadratics, both with constant term $1$ by (ii): $f=(x^2+ax+1)(x^2+bx+1)$. Comparing coefficients: $x^3$: $a+b=1$; $x^2$: $ab+2=1$, so $ab=-1$; $x^1$: $a+b=1$ again. So $a,b$ are the roots of $t^2-t-1$, i.e. $t=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$. In $\mathbb{F}_{29}$, $11^2=121=4\cdot29+5$, so $\sqrt5=\pm11$ and $t=(1+11)/2=6$ or $t=(1-11)/2=-5$. Check: $6+(-5)=1$, $6\cdot(-5)=-30=-1$. Hence
$$x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=(x^2+6x+1)(x^2-5x+1)=(x^2+6x+1)(x^2+24x+1)\quad\text{over }\mathbb{F}_{29},$$
and both factors are irreducible since $f$ has no roots in $\mathbb{F}_{29}$. ∎
